The Life & Times of Hugh Masekela

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We celebrate the life and times of the late-great Hugh Masekela

Unique Selling Point:
With the tragic passing of South African jazz icon Hugh Masekela this week, Carte Blanche looks back at the life and times of a truly great South African through the thoughts and recollections of his friends and colleagues

Summary:
Hugh Masekela is without question one of the greatest South Africans to have ever lived. Small in stature, but with huge talent, he leaves behind a musical legacy that will never be forgotten. Alongside his fellow great contemporaries like Miriam Makeba, Jonas Gwangwa & Caiphus Semenya, he blazed a trail for South African Jazz around the world and became a prominent leading light in the struggle against Apartheid. With his passing from prostate cancer this week, a country mourns the loss of one of it's greatest sons. Tonight on Carte Blanche, we pay tribute to this musical legend through the thoughts and recollections from some of his best friends and colleagues.

Further information:
Through the use of archival material, we celebrate the life and times of the late great Hugh Masekela. We will look back on his biography, from his rise to prominence in the burgeoning South African jazz scene of the 1950's, to his years in exile and his triumphant return to South Africa 30 years later.

We tell Hugh's story through the eyes of his great friends Jonas Gwangwa & Oliver Mtukudzi

We look at the influence he had on the lives of contemporary South African musicians like Kabelo Mabelane, Mi Casa & Simphiwe Dana

We meet collaborators like his photographer Brett Rubin, his stylist Nicole van Heerden and the producer of his final album, No Borders

And we ponder his musical legacy

Press Release:


Hugh Masekela is without question one of the greatest South Africans to have ever lived. Small in stature, but with huge talent, he leaves behind a musical legacy that will never be forgotten. Alongside his fellow great contemporaries like Miriam Makeba, Jonas Gwangwa & Caiphus Semenya, he blazed a trail for South African Jazz around the world and became a prominent leading light in the struggle against Apartheid. With his passing from prostate cancer this week, a country mourns the loss of one of it's greatest sons. Tonight on Carte Blanche, we pay tribute to this musical legend through the thoughts and recollections from some of his best friends and colleagues.

Script:


INTRO VOICE OVER: What makes a man a legend? Is it through years of honing his craft until he becomes master of it? Is it a life story that brought fame & fortune and took him to far-flung places all around the world, until after decades in exile, he was finally able to come back home? Is it the enduring musical legacy he leaves behind, revered by so many as one of the most beloved South Africans of all time?

V/O: Hugh Ramapolo Masekela was born in the coal mining town of Witbank in 1939. Whilst at school in Johannesburg he was mentored by anti-Apartheid priest Trevor Huddleston who gave him his first trumpet. Little did Father Huddleston know the impact his kind act would have on young Hugh, on jazz, South Africa and the world.

Bra Hugh’s great friend Jonas Gwangwa remembers this seminal moment in both of their lives.

Jonas Gwangwa: He was a class ahead of me, we were not really friends until he asked for an instrument from Father Huddleston and he got a trumpet and when I saw that I asked for a trombone. But I wanted a clarinet actually but I just said I wanted a trombone (laughs)

V/O: Hugh & Jonas, began to hone their craft and along with fellow luminaries like Abdullah Ibrahim & Kippie Moeketsi gave birth to the Afro-Jazz sound the world has come to love.

It was a time of great political upheaval in the country. In the shadow of the Sharpville Massacre, 21 year-old Hugh Masekela left South Africa for America upon the invitation of Miriam Makeba. It would be 31 years before he would see his homeland again.

V/O: It was whilst in exile that Hugh Masekela found international fame. Living abroad would shape not only the music he made but also the man he became, as journalist Dudley Moloi explains

Dudley Moloi: But when he went to the US one of the advisors (sic) that he was given was, you know what, there are so many of us here, you pick up a stone and throw it anywhere you'll hit a great musician. The best thing for you to be successful is to stick to your kind of sound. And Bra Hugh listened to that advice, took that advice

V/O: Heeding these wise words, Hugh looked to home for inspiration. The result is a body of work that for many, became the perfect soundtrack for the Anti-Apartheid Struggle

Dudley Moloi: You look at for example, Stimela. You know Stimela is a highly political song, he wrote it while he was in the US.

Hugh Masekela singing: "There's a train that comes from Malawi and Namibia. There's a train that comes from Zambia and Zimbabwe..."

V/O: In his lifetime, Hugh befriended many musicians from all over the world like Zimbabwean guitarist Oliver Mtukudzi with his charm & humility

Oliver Mtukudzi: He's the only artist that flew from South Africa to come to Zimbabwe and get to my home area in the rural areas and paid me a visit, and that far. The guy was humble enough to respect me

V/O: With the advent of democracy in South Africa at the turn of the 90’s Hugh Masekela was at last able to return home.

Now older and wiser, Bra Hugh became a mentor to a new generation of South African musicians like Kabelo Mabalane

Kabelo Mabalane: I got to meet him when I was still in the clutches of addiction and substance abuse. My mother (she didn't actually know Bra Hugh from a bar of soap, it was literally a shot in the dark for her) got hold of Bra Hugh to come speak to me because he was quite open about his struggles with substance abuse.

V/O: For decades he fought his demons and eventually, he won

Jonas Gwangwa: You have to be strong and you have to resist those people. He made a major decision that I'm going to stop. I'm going to stop this with drug and alcohol abuse

Kabelo: He told me if I don't change my life, shared some of his experiences and the rest is history. I'm proud to say I'm also part of Bra Hugh's legacy.

V/O: Songstress Simphiwe Dana remembers the great compassion of Hugh Masekela after her serious car crash

Simphiwe Dana: When I had my accident I was really down in the dumps because you know I had this huge scar on my face, I felt I had lost half of my face. I was already planning ok what is plan B because I'm not going to be able to sing again. I was really feeling sorry for myself and I was just hiding when I came from hospital. Next thing there's a hoot at the gate and Bra Hugh's there and it did something to me, it made me feel like ok, I'm important to legends like Bra Hugh, you know this person that I am that feels very, very small right now is important

V/O: Throughout his life Bra Hugh continued to make music and collaborate with artists, like Mi Casa’s J-Something

J-Something: The more time that I spent with him I just soaked up as much as I could and literally I went back to my room that night, I think it was like the second day we'd been together and I wrote the song in like 5 minutes, I was by everything that he had said. And that song is not about South Africa, it's about Bra Hugh in South Africa.

So the first line in the song is "I left you then I kissed you on my return", obviously Bra Hugh was in exile for 21 years and when he came back he came back with such an appreciation for the country that it felt like he was kissing the country.

J'Something sings: I left you then I kissed you on my return and I watched you from every corner and every curve and I wonder...

V/O: Whilst the nation mourns the passing of one of its greatest sons, it is the family that grieves most. But rather than shed a tear his son Sal Masekela prefers to remember his father’s ebullient laughter most.

Sal Masekela: I mean my memories of my dad are of laughter first at all times. My father had the most infectious laugh on the planet. You know when something really, really hit him, it came from deep you know.

Hugh Masekela: I have to go see Gogo in Epangeni (laughs)

Sal Masekela: He had this manner where he would laugh really ha ha ha ha ha! And then you know he'd do the *click sounds* you know and laugh in his cheeks. And anytime I had the opportunity where I made my father laugh, it was a big deal because he didn't give our laughs for free.

V/O: Perhaps his greatest legacy, more so than his music are the lives he touched so indelibly.

Simphiwe: Dear Bra Hugh, I want to say thank you very much for everything you've done for my generation of musicians and for the past generations

Jonas Gwangwa: Brother, my cousin, my fellow musician, my revolutionary brother, my everything

J'Something: Thank you for making me feel like I was a real superstar and thank you for making me believe in myself in ways that I could never have dreamt of

Oliver Mtukudzi: Your music lives on in us, so you haven't left us

Simphiwe Dana: May you rest in peace, in fact may you fly free

Hugh Masekela: I'm very humble but when you start getting these kind lifetime achievement awards what they're really giving you is like old-people's awards, it means like "hey it's been nice, get out of town!" Laughs
